descriptionChirho: To speak falsehood, tell lies, or deceive verbally in the Piel intensive stem, describing active, deliberate deception by a person. The most frequent sense of this root, appearing in Num 23:19; 2 Kgs 4:16; Job 6:28; 34:6; Ps 78:36; 89:35; Prov 14:5; Isa 57:11; Ezek 13:19; Mic 2:11; Hab 2:3. Multilingual glosses consistently render as lie/deceive: Arabic yakdhibu, German luegen, Korean geojitmal, Hindi jhuth bolna, Spanish mentir.

To fail or prove deceptive, said of things (streams, hopes, visions) that disappoint expectations rather than of persons lying, as in Isa 58:11 where waters do not fail. This is a distinct semantic extension of the Piel where the subject is inanimate and the sense is 'disappoint, prove unreliable' rather than 'tell a falsehood.' Arabic yakdhibu, Spanish faltar.

labelChirho: be found false, be proved a liar (Nifal)
descriptionChirho: To be shown to be false or vain, to be proved a liar, in the Nifal passive/reflexive stem. In Job 41:9 hope of capturing Leviathan is proved vain (nikzbah), and in Prov 30:6 one who adds to God's words will be found a liar (wenikzabta). Arabic yukaddhabu, Korean geojitdweda, Hindi jhutha thahre, Spanish ser hallado mentiroso.

To cause someone to be shown as a liar, to convict of falsehood, in the Hifil causative stem. Occurs in Job 24:25 where Job challenges anyone to prove him a liar (yakzibeni). The causative force distinguishes this from the Piel (active lying) and Nifal (being shown false). Arabic yukaddhibuni, Hindi mujhe jhutha thahraega, Spanish desmentir.

A liar, one who lies, used as a substantive Qal participle describing a person's character or state. In Ps 116:11 'every man is a liar' (kozeb). Functions as a nominal characterization of a person rather than describing an act of lying. Arabic kadhibun, German Luegner, Korean geojitdoeda, Hindi jhutha, Spanish mentiroso.

Falsehoods or lies as a substantive noun (kezabim, plural), the content or product of lying. Found in Judg 16:10,13 where Samson is accused of telling lies (kezabim) to Delilah. This nominal use denotes the lies themselves as objects rather than the verbal act. Arabic kadhibaan, Korean geojitmaldeul, Hindi jhuth, Spanish mentiras.
